title: The holy feasts, reward of the righteous
english: ON ADORATION AND WORSHIP IN SPIRIT AND TRUTH — BOOK SEVENTEEN. On the holy feasts.

Cyril: Let this much be said about purity, about prayers, and indeed about priests. Next, I think, we ought to set out with great care what repayment for their labors would come from God, and by turning toward what they would be enriched with the honors that come at the final allotment, and become sharers in the hope that lasts for ages.
Palladius: How well you put it.

Cyril: For it would be fitting, Palladius, that those who have practiced the glorious and chosen life, and have come so far in conduct, shining here below, that they carry off the best verdict of all, should live in long days of gladness, keeping feast and rejoicing, with Emmanuel as the beginning of their festival, and resting on firmly grounded hopes.
Palladius: It would indeed be fitting, and what you say is true.

Cyril: Shall we, then, look closely into the feasts kept in type and according to the law, and describe the manner of the sacrifices offered at them, carrying over, as far as we can, the force of their meanings into the truth?
Palladius: I would like that; how could I not?

Cyril: Well then, since I think I have reasoned it out clearly and well that, as we ponder these things too, we ought to judge them with care, come, come, let us first of all search out when, and on what occasions, the sacred Writing said that we must keep feast. For in this way our discussion would go straight along the fitting road; and besides, it will nobly ward off any appearance of having been put together without art.

title: Three feasts a year, and Pharaoh's refusal
english: Palladius: Go on, then, wherever you please; you will do me good, and very richly.

Cyril: Once, when those of Israel had been gathered in the wilderness below Mount Horeb, the God of all laid down for us the law that marks out what we must do. And after he had commanded countless decrees, and profitable ones, he then added: ‘Three times a year keep a feast to me’ (Exodus 23:14). What these times were he made clear in turn, for he said at once: ‘Take care to keep the feast of unleavened bread. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the season of the month of new grain; for in it you came out of Egypt. You shall not appear before me empty. And you shall keep the feast of the harvest of the firstfruits of your labors, of whatever you sow in your field, and the feast of completion at the end of the year, when you gather in your labors from your field. Three times a year every male of yours shall appear before the Lord your God’ (Exodus 23:15–17).

That keeping the feasts for God would be most fitting for those who play the man, and not rather for those who are slack and have a feeble mind in them, always softened toward the things of the flesh and of the world, he showed by saying: ‘Three times a year every male of yours shall appear before the Lord your God.’ For what is male is worthy of oversight from above and from God, in the ways already described. Yet he legislated usefully that holy feasts must be kept. For it was needful, truly needful, to show very plainly to those who were climbing to the beginning of a right training, and were already somehow coming under the yoke of God, the end of the life under the law: that in every way and at all events it would end for them in delights and gladness, plainly spiritual ones. That is why, after he had proclaimed the law, had neatly set apart what by its nature does wrong, had praised what leads to profit, and had set before them the way of the conduct and life that pleases him, he let them understand that their labor would one day end in delights. So the first feast is in the month of new grain; the second, a close neighbor, comes at once, the feast of the harvest of the firstfruits; and the third and last is the feast at the end of the year, when our fruits have been gathered in, in the seventh month of the year. Or is that not what the sacred Writing said?
Palladius: I agree.

Cyril: Then we must bring forward what belongs to each season, and examine, as far as we can, how and on what grounds it is fitting for it to be kept. At that time the compassionate God was commanding those of Israel to depart from the land of the Egyptians, to throw off the yoke of an unbearable servitude, and to move across to the land of promise. But Pharaoh set himself against what had been decreed. He let loose a boorish word against the ineffable glory, saying, ‘I do not know the Lord’ (Exodus 5:2), and he declared again and again that he would not let those of Israel go; and so he was punished with plague upon plague, one after another. But since he was still unyielding, and his unbroken…

title: The destroyer in Egypt and the law of the Passover lamb
english: Cyril: …madness he kept up against God, the one who holds authority over all let loose the destroyer on the firstborn of the Egyptians, and passed sentence of death on them in a single night. But he took care beforehand that the flocks of the Jews should not fall under the evil, and should be as far as possible from the hand, or rather the wrath, of the destroyer. Yet this could be done for anyone in no other way than through Christ, who is life and gives life, since he was begotten of the one who is life by nature, the Father. So the law sketched in advance the mystery concerning him, and speaks thus:

‘The Lord said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt: This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it is the first for you among the months of the year. Speak to all the congregation of the sons of Israel, saying: On the tenth of this month let each man take a sheep by their fathers' houses, each man a sheep for a household. And if there are too few in the household to be enough for a sheep, he shall take with him his neighbor who is near him, according to the number of souls; each shall be counted toward the sheep according to what is enough for him. Your sheep shall be perfect, male, a year old; you shall take it from the lambs and from the kids. And it shall be kept by you until the fourteenth day of this month, and the whole multitude of the congregation of the sons of Israel shall slaughter it toward evening. And they shall take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and on the lintel, in the houses in which they eat them. And they shall eat the meat that night, roasted with fire, and they shall eat unleavened bread with bitter herbs. You shall not eat any of it raw, nor boiled in water, but only roasted with fire, the head with the feet and the inward parts. None of it shall be left until morning, and you shall not break a bone of it; and what is left of it until morning you shall burn with fire. And this is how you shall eat it: your loins girded, your sandals on your feet, and your staffs in your hands; and you shall eat it in haste. It is the Lord's Passover. And I will pass through the land of Egypt on this night, and I will strike every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from man to beast, and on all the gods of the Egyptians I will execute judgment: I am the Lord. And the blood shall be for you a sign on the houses in which you are; and I will see the blood and shelter you, and there shall be no plague among you to destroy you when I strike in the land of Egypt. And this day shall be a memorial for you, and you shall keep it as a feast to the Lord throughout all your generations; you shall keep it as an everlasting ordinance. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, and from the first day you shall remove leaven from your houses. Whoever eats leaven, that soul shall be utterly destroyed from Israel, from the first day until the seventh day. And the first day shall be called holy, and the seventh day shall be a holy convocation for you; you shall do no work of service on them, except what must be done for every soul; this alone shall be done by you’ (Exodus 12:1–16).
Would you like us, then, closely and yet briefly…
translator_notes: Exodus 12:10: Cyril's Greek, like the LXX, has 'and you shall not break a bone of it' already here; the Hebrew has it at 12:46.

title: The new age in Christ and the one house of the Church
english: Cyril: …going through each point, should we say what is fitting? For we will ‘give the wise an occasion, and make things known to the righteous,’ as it is written (Proverbs 9:9); and they too may add what is their own, and they will be far better for it.
Palladius: Very much so.

Cyril: Well then, at the beginning of the year and in the first month the mystery of Christ is revealed. For a new age has come to us, the time of our Savior's coming among us, which changes all things for the better and very well refashions into a newness of creation what was growing old and aging and near to vanishing (Hebrews 8:13). ‘For the things in Christ are a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new’ (2 Corinthians 5:17). And we ourselves live no longer in the manner of Moses; we have been carried over, rather, into the life of the gospel, since Christ makes us new through the Spirit.
Palladius: You are right.

Cyril: Each man takes the sheep, and the diners gather in numbers into one house. For we too, divided as we are by nature into separate existence one by one, have run together into spiritual unity in Christ; for from now on there is one soul in us, and one heart (Acts 4:32). The victim is a sheep, or else one from the goats. A sheep, because of its incomparable gentleness and innocence, and besides this its fruitfulness: ‘For he was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent’ (Isaiah 53:7). A lamb, because he was sacrificed for us and handed over for our sins, according to the Scriptures. A kid, because by the law that is the sacrifice offered for sins. The sheep is perfect and male. ‘Perfect’ signifies that it is free from every blemish, strong and healthy; for Christ is without blemish and beyond every passion, which is to say truly perfect, since Emmanuel is all-perfect, having of himself and by nature all that makes him God. ‘Male’ signifies that he is the leader of all; for the male is always the more governing, and the female everywhere in the second rank.

The sheep is taken from the tenth of the month, but it is offered toward evening on the fourteenth. For the mystery of Christ is not newly come to light, nor was it first recognized when the Jews thought fit to treat him with drunken violence. The knowledge of it went far ahead of the suffering, since the saints foretold it, the law cried it aloud, and Holy Scripture sketched in advance for us the mystery concerning him. So for the time being we held it among ourselves as foreknowledge: the lamb not yet sacrificed, but we were not unaware that it would be slaughtered toward evening. For it was in the last times of the age, when time was already somehow reaching its very setting, that the death of Christ was accomplished. And it is slaughtered by the whole multitude, for he died for all; so that those who offer the lamb for their own salvation may know that they were bought with a price and are not their own (1 Corinthians 6:19–20), but that ‘one died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them and was raised’ (2 Corinthians 5:14–15). For since…

title: One night of suffering, and a lamb neither raw nor boiled
english: Cyril: …he was handed over for our trespasses, he is said to have died because of us. That is why we too are the ones who slaughter it. For those on whose account he necessarily died would plainly be, all but, the doers of the suffering, even if something was done by the hands of others. That the sprinkling of the blood saves those who have been anointed with it, he showed at once by saying that the entrances of the rooms must be smeared with the blood, I mean the doorposts and the lintels of the doors. For the mystery of Christ blocks the entrance against death and makes it, as it were, impassable to it. It stands firm, then, that we too, anointed with the precious blood, will be stronger than death and will think nothing of corruption, making no account of the destroyer. For the blood of life, that is, of Christ, rescues us.

He says that the flesh of the lamb must be consumed in a single night. For truly the time of the saving suffering is one; and ‘having died once, he dies no more,’ as it is written; ‘death will no longer have dominion over him. For the death he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life he lives, he lives to God’ (Romans 6:9–10). The flesh is roasted, and it is eaten with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. The roasting hints at the perfecting, so to speak, of Emmanuel through sufferings: ‘For it was fitting, truly fitting,’ it says, ‘to make the author of our salvation perfect through sufferings’ (Hebrews 2:10). Its being eaten with unleavened bread and bitter herbs sketches in a riddle that we ourselves, before whom Christ is set to share, must be rid of the leaven of the mind, that is, of malice and deceit, and must love above all to endure suffering for love of him and to bear bitter labors, following after the one who for our sake went into death. To spur us on to this he says: ‘A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master’ (Matthew 10:24). ‘If they persecuted me, they will persecute you too’ (John 15:20). ‘If they called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more those of his household’ (Matthew 10:25).

Then the law forbids eating it raw, and boiled in water as well, although no one, I think, would have eaten it raw even if the law had not happened to say so. So it suggests in a riddle that the mystery of Christ has neither the repulsiveness that comes from an excess of falsehoods nor anything watery and slack. For the choice poets and prose writers of the Greeks, and all who were wise as far as words go, when they record the rites of their gods, tell outrageous lies and serve up to human minds tales that are, so to speak, raw and unacceptable; and much that is watery and sickly has a hold among them. Adulteries and passions for women, the corruption of boys, the cutting off of private parts, maidens changed into trees, and other things besides, utterly shameful and ugly: these are the little myths they believe. But all that is in Christ is truth, easily received and good food for the mind, with nothing slack or watery in it. For it draws those who are willing to understand toward good order, rather than letting them loose into luxury and love of the flesh, as the Greeks'…
translator_notes: Hebrews 2:10 is quoted in Cyril's own form ('it was needful, needful'), not the epistle's 'it was fitting'.

title: Head, feet, and inward parts as Christ's mind, way, and mysteries
english: Cyril: …cold old wives' tales do. Do you understand clearly, then, what I mean?
Palladius: Certainly.

Cyril: That whoever has become a sharer in Christ, through partaking of his holy flesh and blood, must also have his mind, and love to go forward through inward achievements, understanding very well what concerns him, he would have shown at once by saying that the head must be eaten with the feet and the inward parts. For did we not say that the head is a type of the mind, and that the feet everywhere signify our course, as it were, in deeds? And did the inward parts of the victims not point in turn to what is within and hidden?
Palladius: That did seem the right way to understand it. But tell me this: what would be Christ's mind, what his course, and what the hidden things?

Cyril: Christ's mind would be to think only of whatever looks toward the glory of God the Father, and to wish to accomplish what seems good to the one who begot him. ‘For I have come down from heaven,’ he says, ‘not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me’ (John 6:38). Having chosen to think this and to accomplish it, the inspired disciples too said plainly, ‘But we have the mind of Christ’ (1 Corinthians 2:16). And so they taught us to say in prayers: ‘Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your will; your kingdom come; your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth’ (Matthew 6:9–10). Do you see that, having become of one purpose and one mind with Christ, they plainly affirm that they have his mind? This, I think, is the eating of the lamb's head.

Christ's course, for its part, is to endure nobly what was his to bear, and not to shrink from death, so that, as Paul says, he might save sinners (1 Timothy 1:15). And it befits us too to be most ready for this, readily spending even our life in the body for our brothers. So one of the holy disciples said: ‘Since therefore Christ suffered for us in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same thought for his sake’ (1 Peter 4:1). Paul, for his part, rebukes some, speaking somewhat like this: ‘Why are you weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound, but even to die for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ’ (Acts 21:13). And Christ himself, bidding us follow in his own footsteps, says: ‘Whoever does not take up his cross daily and follow after me is not worthy of me’ (Matthew 10:38). Holy also in every other respect, and through every virtue, is Christ's course and way.

By the inward parts you will understand the account of him that is hidden and kept in secret. For being God by nature, and having appeared from God, the Only-begotten became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14); and being the image and likeness of the one who begot him, he let himself down into self-emptying and into the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7). Let us, then, receive into our own souls not only what is…
translator_notes: The Greek prints the Lord's Prayer as 'hallowed be your will' (θέλημα), where Matthew 6:9 has 'your name'; translated as printed.
The saying on taking up the cross is Matthew 10:38 with 'daily' as in Luke 9:23.

title: Nothing left until morning, and no bone of the lamb broken
english: Cyril: …human and outwardly visible in Emmanuel; but if we also fill our own mind with his very inward parts, that is, with his hidden mysteries, we shall have spiritual nourishment.

He said, moreover, that the lamb must be consumed in that one night, nothing at all being left over and remaining until morning; and he does not allow even a bone to be broken. The first signifies that in the age to come Christ will sanctify and bless those devoted to him through faith and holiness in some other way: he will surely not again nourish them with his own flesh and give them life by his blood, as he of course does now; rather, since death will already have been abolished and corruption wholly undone, the manner of the one who sanctifies will be a spiritual one. So the morning would signify, I think, nothing other than the age to come. The second, I mean that the bone must not be broken, lifts us up to the thoughts that concern Christ and persuades us to follow the voices of those who speak of God. For the inspired evangelist, taking the oracle in a more bodily sense of Christ, says: ‘The soldiers did not break his legs, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled: Not a bone of him shall be broken’ (John 19:33–36).

They eat the lamb with their loins girded, their feet shod, and staffs in their hands; in short, dressed like people who are used to traveling; and very rightly. For as people made ready to move on in spirit, pressing, as it were, to travel out of the distractions of this world, and eager to pass over to whatever is best, we shall partake of Christ in all holiness and purity. For we are not used to lingering over things that pass; we run nobly toward what is fixed and abiding; and setting out from the impurities of the flesh, we leap across to spiritual refinement, remembering that Christ said, ‘Rise, let us go from here’ (John 14:31). That is why those who eat the lamb as a type of Christ wear the dress that fits travelers.

But it must be eaten in haste. For it is the Lord's Passover, that is, a crossing, or the rites of crossing. For when the time has come in which we must cross over from worldly baseness and hasten to do what pleases God, not to do this with all haste, but to delay and hang back, as it were, still clinging to our old evils, how would that not be most perilous? So the inspired Paul says, ‘Run, so that you may obtain it’ (1 Corinthians 9:24). We must go, then, to partake of Christ through faith, with all sluggishness trampled underfoot and no delay slipping in, but with all haste. For so we shall cross from sins to justification, from death to life; and rubbing off the shame of slavery, we shall be enriched with the glorious grace of adoption.

title: The firstborn struck, leaven put away, and the holy first and seventh days
english: Palladius: You have spoken excellently.

Cyril: When these things have been carefully kept, and indeed carried through to the end as the lawgiver wished, he says that he will pass through and, as it were, go about the whole land of the Egyptians, destroying the firstborn and executing judgment on the gods of the Egyptians; that is, he will exact a penalty from all that was lofty and exalted among them and ranked all but among the objects of worship because of its glory, for so harsh and lawless a mind and for overweening arrogance. But he promised to shelter the sons of Israel, since their lintels had been smeared with the blood, which he also called a sign of their belonging to him: ‘For I will see the sign,’ he says, ‘and I will shelter you’ (Exodus 12:13). For when God brings wrath and anger on everything lofty and high, as the prophet's word has it (Isaiah 2:12), and condemns to death the wanton sinner who has endlessly neglected reverence toward him, only those escape and have no share in the punishment who have been sealed with the good seal and sprinkled with the blood of Christ. For you have heard him say: ‘Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life (John 6:54), and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life (John 5:24); but whoever does not believe will not see life, but the wrath of God will remain on him’ (John 3:36). So those who have been sanctified through partaking of Christ, in the mystical manner of course, and anointed with the holy blood, are sharers in eternal life, friends and intimates of God the Father, and stronger than death.

He says, and very well, that they must press on without ceasing to carry out the law on this point. For surely we shall not cease from keeping feast in Christ as we remove leaven from our own borders, that is, from all the land in which we spend our days. For those called through faith to the justification that comes through Christ, as they keep feast spiritually, must not do this in the leaven of malice and wickedness; rather, they must clean out the old leaven (1 Corinthians 5:7–8), be refashioned for the better, and be seen already, in some way, as a new lump, with all their kin and all their household, and those in all the land; by which it is signified that the holy multitude of those who have received the faith is great and beyond counting.

He said that the first day of the week must be called holy, and the seventh too a holy convocation. By this, I think, the law shows that in the life of man the time at the beginning was holy, as in Adam, the forefather of the race, before he had broken what was commanded and disregarded the divine precepts; and holy, and much greater, is the time at the end, that is, the time in Christ, who is the second Adam, refashioning the race, from what had happened in between, into newness of life in the Spirit. He also enjoins that one must keep sabbath on the seventh day, ceasing from all work. For it would very fittingly befit those who through faith have en…
translator_notes: Cyril joins John 6:54, 5:24 and 3:36 into a single saying.

title: Hyssop, the blood, and staying indoors until morning
english: Cyril: … into the rest of Christ, from then on to keep away from every work of the flesh, from earthly pursuits and idle running about, and to hasten instead to accomplish only what leads to the undefiled life and makes people venerable and holy. For as the wise Paul writes to us, ‘Whoever has entered his rest’ (that is, clearly, Christ’s) ‘has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his own’ (Hebrews 4:10).
Palladius: True.

Cyril: This, then, is what the divine oracle told us. And when the divine Moses was laying the command before the sons of Israel, he said, ‘Go and take for yourselves a sheep according to your families, and sacrifice the Passover. And you shall take a bunch of hyssop, and dip it in some of the blood that is by the door, and put it on the lintel and on both doorposts, some of the blood that is by the door. And none of you shall go out of the door of his house until morning. And the Lord will pass by to strike the Egyptians, and he will see the blood on the lintel and on both doorposts, and the Lord will pass by the door, and he will not let the destroyer come into your houses to strike’ (Exodus 12:21–23).

That the lamb is to be taken by fathers’ houses, that is, by families, would indicate, I think, the sameness of spiritual kinship, as in faith and in concord. For we shall not keep the feast together with those who have chosen to hold perverted views, nor shall we share the holy and life-giving sacrifice with those accustomed to think things other than what is right and true, but with those who are of one mind with us and are our brothers, as in unity of spirit and in sameness of faith.

The hyssop, moreover, is joined by design with the blood of the lamb. What the reason for this might be, I will tell in a few words. Hyssop, Palladius, is said to be a herb, and the physicians admire it as well able to melt away, and very vigorously, the impurity in the inward parts, and to thin out thoroughly the clotted masses of phlegm, because of the strength of the natural heat that is in it. So the blood is joined to the hyssop, as I said just now, the type showing us indirectly that the precious blood of Christ frees us not only from corruption but also from all impurity hidden within, and does not let us cool off into sloth, but makes us rather fervent in spirit (Romans 12:11).

And that it is necessary and profitable for those once counted worthy to share in Christ to love to keep the life of holiness secure and never to leave it, the law indicates again by seating within the doors those who had eaten the lamb, so that they might not be destroyed along with the Egyptians by going out of their houses. For it is not right to doubt that anyone at all of those counted among the sanctified, who has, as a kind of house, …
translator_notes: Cyril’s Exodus 12:21 reads ‘a sheep’ (πρόβατον) where the rest of the passage speaks of the lamb.

title: This age as night, and Christ our Passover
english: Cyril: … virtue, if he should somehow depart from holiness, will perish along with the rest and will be subject together to the penalties that would be brought on those who have fallen sick with the licentious and incurable life. That is why the inspired Psalmist says to us, ‘Do not destroy my soul with the ungodly, nor my life with men of blood, in whose hands are lawless deeds’ (Psalm 26:9–10). See, then, how it says, ‘You shall not go out of the door of your house until morning’ (Exodus 12:22). For the sacred letter likens the present age to night, and the age to come, which we expect, to day. Indeed the blessed Paul, seeing the present age already drawing to its end and the age to come close by, all but at the doors already, called out, saying, ‘The night is far gone, the day is at hand. So let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light; let us walk becomingly, as in the day’ (Romans 13:12–13). ‘Until morning,’ then, would signify the whole of life, that is, until the coming season is made manifest. And how would this happen for us? At the end of each one’s life the age to come has all but entered; if indeed it is true that the one who has gone down into death has been set free from sin (Romans 6:7), for God has shut him in, as it is written, and he is kept for the judgment seat of Christ, and as he was when his own end overtook him, so he will stand there.
Palladius: I understand what you say; and the argument is very good indeed.

Cyril: In this way, then, the mystery of Christ was sketched in shadow for the people of old, when the lamb was sacrificed at its season, the very season at which Emmanuel himself truly underwent slaughter for the life of all. The inspired Paul indeed writes that ‘Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed for us’ (1 Corinthians 5:7). Yet the divine oracle said that the sacred rites must be performed in the second month too, and the form of the feast carried through, if some necessary hindrance should happen to shut us out and keep us from being able to fulfill in the first month what was decreed. Would you like us to set out the divine saying itself and then say what is fitting?
Palladius: By all means.

Cyril: It is written, then, in Numbers: ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses on Mount Sinai in the second year after they had come out of the land of Egypt, in the first month, saying: Speak, and let the sons of Israel keep the Passover at its season, on the fourteenth day of the first month, toward evening; you shall keep it at its appointed time; according to its law and according to its ordinance you shall keep it. And Moses told the sons of Israel to keep the Passover, beginning on the fourteenth day of the month, in the wilderness of Sinai. As the Lord had commanded Moses, so the sons of Israel did’ (Numbers 9:1–5).
translator_notes: Cyril’s Numbers 9:1 reads ‘on Mount Sinai’; the Septuagint has ‘in the wilderness of Sinai’.
‘For God has shut him in, as it is written’ may echo Genesis 7:16.

title: God's second season of mercy for the unclean
english: Cyril: … ‘And there came the men who were unclean through a human soul, and they could not keep the Passover on that day. And they came before Moses and Aaron on that day, and those men said to him: We are unclean through a human soul; must we then be kept back from offering the gift to the Lord at its season among the sons of Israel? And Moses said to them: Stand here, and I will hear what the Lord will command concerning you. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel, saying: Any man who becomes unclean through a human soul, or is on a journey far from you, or among your generations, and would keep the Passover to the Lord: in the second month, on the fourteenth day, toward evening, they shall keep it; with unleavened bread and bitter herbs they shall eat it by night; they shall leave none of it until morning, and they shall not break a bone of it. According to the law of the Passover they shall keep it. And the man who is clean and is not on a journey far away, and fails to keep the Passover, that soul shall be destroyed from its people, because he did not offer the gift to the Lord at its season; that man shall bear his sin. And if a proselyte comes to you in your land and keeps the Passover to the Lord according to the law of the Passover and according to its ordinance, so shall he keep it. There shall be one law for you, both for the proselyte and for the native of the land’ (Numbers 9:6–14).
Palladius: And who might they be, who are unclean as through a human soul and make this a pretext for not being able to keep the Passover? I should like to know clearly, you may be sure.

Cyril: The account of the history is a very long one. I will recall God crying out to Moses, the revealer of sacred things: ‘Speak to the sons of Israel, and let them send out of the camp every leper and everyone who has a discharge, and everyone unclean through a soul’ (Numbers 5:2). We have already labored over the account of these things enough. But I will say this, as useful for the present. By ‘unclean through a human soul’ the sacred letter means the one defiled by a corpse. For it was forbidden even to touch a lifeless body, and the ancient decree laid the charge of uncleanness on those mourning one of their near kin and blood. That is why they were sent out of the camp. And by these things the law foreshadowed that whoever has shared in another’s deadness, in character and ways, will be unholy and full of spiritual uncleanness. For those are dead in their ways of whom Christ would say, ‘Let the dead bury their own dead’ (Matthew 8:22). So the one who has shared with those used to thinking and doing dead things, or has even come near them (I mean by choosing to think and do the same), is to be sent outside the divine court, and the Church of the firstborn (Hebrews 12:23), and the flock of the saints. Such, then, is the riddle of the law. But by the true sense, and the one most fitting for us who are spiritual, those unclean through a human soul, who for this reason keep the feast in the …

title: The second-month Passover, and the danger of not keeping the feast
english: Cyril: … second month, slaughtering the victim as a type of Christ according to the law of the Passover, we shall take to be none other than the Jews, defiled by the murder of Christ and having as the charge that makes them unclean their drunken outrage against Emmanuel. Such people, of necessity, slipped away from our holy feast. They come late, and have missed the season at which the author of the life of all was made perfect through sufferings (Hebrews 2:10). Yet by the mercy of the one who wills to save all (1 Timothy 2:4), in the times after this, as in a second month, they too will share in Christ and will keep the feast with the saints called at the proper time, that is, clearly, with those from the nations. For see how the people in Egypt at once rubbed off the filth of idolatry, slaughtered the lamb in the first month, and sprang up to the beginnings of faith. Those anointed with the blood of the Lord will count the destroyer as nothing and will prove stronger than corruption. But the others, as in the second year and in the second month, barely come at last and confess their defilement. They affirmed plainly that they had become unclean through a human soul, and they ask to be given the blessing; and later, after the first, they fulfill the feast. ‘For when the fullness of the nations has come in,’ it says, ‘then all Israel will be saved’ (Romans 11:25–26). And the prophet foretold about them somewhere: ‘And after these things the sons of Israel will return and will seek the Lord their God and David their king, and they will be amazed at the Lord and at his good things in the last days’ (Hosea 3:5). For in the last times Christ, of the seed of David according to the flesh, will be sought by those who are left of Israel.
Palladius: The word is true; for Israel has been set in hope.

Cyril: That it is not without fault, or rather that it is among the most perilous things of all, not to keep the feasts in Christ’s honor, he made clear at once, when he said that the one who is neither unclean through a human soul nor on a long journey, and has no necessary hindrance, will be brought under the utmost penalties if he does not choose to do what is prescribed. By the one unclean as through a human soul we may understand, as we were saying just now, the Jew who killed the Lord. And as on a long journey and somewhere outside Jerusalem, that is, the holy Church of our Savior, is ‘the one who says to the wood, You are my God, and to the stone, You have begotten me’ (Jeremiah 2:27); and also the one who worships the creation rather than the Creator (Romans 1:25), or anyone sick with some other error. For it is true that every good man is understood to be near God, holding a pure and undebased belief about him, while everyone who is not so has stood aside, withdrawn, and is far off. So we who are neither unclean through a human soul, like the Jews, nor on a long journey, like the pagans or the heretics, will earnestly and without delay offer the sacrifice and honor the feasts of the Lord.

title: The convert at the table, and the Passover kept in the Church
english: Cyril: … And the proselyte will keep the feast with you under the same law and will share the joy of those who rejoice. For those who at the right times accept the glories of faith in Christ we make partners in the bloodless sacrifice, and we call them to share in the holy table. And I think it necessary to add this as well: a custom has prevailed in the churches, taken, I think, from this very law, that if the fourteenth day of the moon falls outside the first month, the second month, the one next to it, is examined, and the appointed day is sought in it, so that the true season of the feast may not slip away. That is how the matter stands, just as it was laid down beforehand in the ancient law.

Palladius: You have spoken rightly. But tell me this. Did the law perhaps allow anyone at all, even if he were on a long journey and as far as possible from Jerusalem, to keep the Passover without blame?

Cyril: Certainly not. It commanded the sacrifice to be made only in the holy city, the city in which Solomon also built the ancient temple. Moses addressed the sons of Israel in Deuteronomy as follows: ‘Observe the month of the new crops, and you shall keep the Passover to the Lord your God, because in the month of the new crops you came out of Egypt by night. And you shall sacrifice the Passover to the Lord your God, sheep and oxen, in the place which the Lord your God chooses, for his name to be called upon there. You shall not eat leaven with it. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread with it, the bread of affliction, because you came out of Egypt in haste, so that you may remember the day of your departure from the land of Egypt all the days of your life. No leaven shall be seen with you in all your borders for seven days, and none of the meat which you sacrifice in the evening on the first day shall be left overnight until morning. You may not sacrifice the Passover in any of your cities which the Lord your God gives you, but only at the place which the Lord your God chooses, for his name to be called upon there. You shall sacrifice the Passover in the evening, at the setting of the sun, at the time when you came out of Egypt; and you shall boil and roast and eat it in the place which the Lord your God chooses’ (Deuteronomy 16:1–7).

The land of the Jews was filled with countless cities and villages, yet God prescribed that the sacred rites and the law of the Passover must be fulfilled in the holy city alone. In this, I think, the letter of the law sketches very well for us that it would not be right, nor is it allowed to anyone, to fulfill the mystery of Christ in whatever way he pleases, or in any place at all. For the only place fitting for it, and truly most proper to it, is the holy city, that is, the Church, in which there is a lawful priest, and the sacred rites are performed by sanctified hands, and incense is offered to God who rules over all, and a pure sacrifice, as the prophet’s voice says (Malachi 1:11). So in no way do they keep the …
translator_notes: ‘The proselyte will keep the feast with you under the same law’ restates Numbers 9:14 in Cyril’s own words.

title: Heretics who seize the priesthood, and the Passover offerings
english: Cyril: … law on this point, those heretics who twist what is right. For they sacrifice the lamb not in the holy city, nor by the hands of those chosen through the Spirit for sacred service, but, as the divine Paul writes to us, they seize the honor for themselves (Hebrews 5:4) and offer in every place. Like insolent and unruly bulls they charge without discernment at whatever alone seems good to them. But they, practicing so much unbridled license and a bent toward madness, will pay a bitter penalty to the judge of such schemes. Let us go back again to the well-worn and straight path, and examine this point in the law that was cited. You heard it say clearly, ‘Observe the month of the new crops, and you shall keep the Passover to the Lord your God, sheep and oxen’ (Deuteronomy 16:1–2). And yet why, someone might say, when he laid down the law of the Passover for those in Egypt, did he command only one lamb to be sacrificed, while we shall not find him mentioning sheep and calves? Did Moses, then, miss what was fitting? Not at all. For in Numbers God made a further law, that oxen and sheep be brought in addition to the lamb, saying, ‘And in the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, is the Passover to the Lord. And on the fifteenth day of this month is a feast; for seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. And the first day shall be called holy for you; you shall do no servile work. And you shall offer whole burnt offerings, an offering by fire to the Lord: two calves from the herd, one ram, seven lambs a year old; they shall be without blemish for you. And their sacrifice shall be fine flour mixed with oil: three tenths for the one calf, and two tenths for the one ram. You shall make a tenth, a tenth for each lamb, for the seven lambs; and one male goat for sin, to make propitiation for you; besides the continual whole burnt offering of the morning, which is a whole burnt offering of perpetuity. In this way you shall make these each day for the seven days, a gift, an offering by fire for a fragrant aroma to the Lord; besides the continual whole burnt offering you shall make its drink offering. And the seventh day shall be called holy for you; you shall do no servile work on it’ (Numbers 28:16–25).

That the Passover must be kept, according to the law, in the first month, and on the fourteenth day, we have already said earlier. And what the eating of unleavened bread would mean, and the rest on the sabbath, and besides that the naming of both the first day and the seventh as ‘called holy’, our discussion has already shown clearly. So, ceasing to linger any longer over these, let us go once more to the manners of the sacrifices. There are, then, two calves for whole burnt offerings and sacrifice, one ram, and lambs to the number of seven, all without blemish and a year old; and the sacrifice with them is fine flour mixed with oil, but not in equal measure: three tenths for each calf, two for the ram, and one for each of the lambs. Then a male goat is brought in with them for sin. ‘And all these,’ it says,…

title: Christ's death bearing much fruit, and the offerings that follow
english: Cyril: … ‘besides the continual whole burnt offerings’ (Numbers 28:23). Behold, then, Palladius, the death of Emmanuel bearing fruit in many, according to what he said clearly and truly: ‘Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit’ (John 12:24). For the lamb is slaughtered as a type of Christ, in the first month according to the law, on the fourteenth day. And calves and a ram and lambs are added for sacrifice and whole burnt offerings, signifying in a type, I think, both the multitude of those called through faith to holiness and the measure of their spiritual vigor. For if Christ had not died for you, we would not have been received as a fragrant aroma by God the Father. But since he has been made perfect through sufferings, we follow straight after him, bringing ourselves to God the Father as an offering fit for holy things, and as a truly spiritual sacrifice.

There are two calves, then, because there are two peoples: I mean Israel and those from the nations. And there is one ram, because we are made one in Christ, ‘who made both one, and broke down the dividing wall of the fence, and abolished the law of commandments in ordinances, so that he might create the two into one new man, making peace’ (Ephesians 2:14–15), as it is written. And the lambs were seven: for all of us who have become one in Christ are a broad flock, running under the hand of the one chief shepherd of all, gathered somehow already from two flocks into one; and, distinguished by a pure and blameless life, we live on in the world because of the one who for us endured slaughter among the lawless (Isaiah 53:12) and for the sin of all, who is also signified in the male goat. And in mentioning a calf and a ram and a lamb, the law indicated the three degrees of the God-loving life of the saints: the highest, I mean, the middle, and the one still lower and inferior. For in the bodily sizes of the animals the amount of spiritual vigor was depicted. Did not the word of the gospel way of life also say that the most fertile soil gives its fruit in three degrees?
Palladius: Yes. ‘One,’ it says, ‘yielded a hundredfold, another sixty, another thirty’ (Matthew 13:8).

Cyril: It is settled, then, that the difference in virtue and the variety of life are well sketched as in the number of the victims and in their bodily bulk: the highest and surpassing degree, as in the calf; the middle, falling below the perfect, as in the smaller ram; and the one still lower, as in the yet smaller lamb. For the lamb is smaller than the ram, just as, of course, the ram is smaller than the calf. Therefore the measure of fine flour, which is a type of life, is added in proportion to the size of each: three tenths for the calf, two for the ram, and one for the lamb. But he said that all of it must be moistened with oil, for the gifts from God will surely follow in proportion to each one’s measure. And in the life of glory and blessedness there will be a great difference. To some the highest will fittingly belong, to others one of a lesser degree, yet in honor and glory, and to some…
translator_notes: Cyril writes ‘if Christ had not died for you’ and goes on with ‘we’; the change of person is in the Greek.

title: Differing glories of the saints and the Church's unceasing fragrance
english: Cyril: … a lower and still humbler one. ‘For star differs from star in glory’ (1 Corinthians 15:41). Even among the holy angels themselves, I say, the measure of glory comes in many degrees; yet whatever the measure, the life of the saints is full of gladness, and they must be of good cheer and be richly fed with the gifts of God. For see how the oil was poured not only on the three tenths, but on the two and on the one as well. And the lamb slaughtered in the holy tent in the morning and again toward evening he calls the sacrifice and whole burnt offerings of perpetuity. From this, again, we may learn that great is the fragrance of the holy tent, and truly unceasing is the sweet savor of the churches and of the saints in them. For they give off the fragrance of Emmanuel and perform the mystery of Christ, bringing the bloodless worship to God. This, I think, is what the offering of the lambs as whole burnt offerings in the morning and toward evening means: by the beginning and the end, what lies between is understood as well. So from first to last there is fragrance in the churches, as in the lamb, Christ.
Palladius: Well said.

Cyril: To the first feast the law joins another, and all but links the very seasons together for us, saying in Numbers: ‘And on the day of the new crops, when you offer a new sacrifice of weeks to the Lord, it shall be called holy for you; you shall do no servile work. And you shall offer whole burnt offerings for a fragrant aroma to the Lord: two calves from the herd, one ram, seven lambs a year old, without blemish. Their sacrifice shall be fine flour mixed with oil: three tenths for the one calf, and two tenths for the one ram, a tenth, a tenth for each lamb, for the seven lambs; and one male goat for sin, to make propitiation for you, besides the continual whole burnt offering. And you shall make their sacrifice for me (they shall be without blemish for you), and their drink offerings’ (Numbers 28:26–31).

In the first month, by the laws of the Hebrews, the lamb was slaughtered. In the next, the neighboring month perhaps, it was the custom to gather in the produce of the fields, I mean the early pulses, and the sheaf, once the wheat had been reaped. So this is the season of the new crops, at which what was sown in the fields must be gathered in. And such a feast, he says, is ‘called’ as well, and it is to be carried through according to the law, free from toil and sweat. For it is the custom at feasts to rest and to keep as far as possible from the more laborious kinds of work. And from this one might learn again that for those who keep a holy feast to God it would be least of all fitting to commit inglorious and utterly wicked sin; rather they should, as it were, rest and fill the mind, and take their delight in the pursuits of virtue. And there are offered as whole burnt offering and sacrifice two calves, one ram and seven lambs, fine flour moistened with oil, and a male goat. Where the riddle of the law points, we explained just now; we will not repeat ourselves. But this we must say: that of our Savior’s resurrection …
translator_notes: ‘Called’ (κλητή) picks up the law’s phrase ‘called holy’ for the feast days.

title: The feast of new fruits as a figure of the resurrection
english: Cyril: …the season of the new crops reproduces the mystery in type. For human nature blossomed anew in Christ first, having rubbed off corruption and cast away, from then on, the oldness that came from sin. That is why it gloried greatly in this, saying: ‘Let my soul exult in the Lord; for he has clothed me with a garment of salvation and a tunic of gladness’ (Isaiah 61:10). By a garment of salvation, and indeed a robe of gladness, it surely meant incorruption, the incorruption from above, from heaven, and in Christ. And he set out more clearly the law for this festival as well, and through a great many details made the riddle plain, saying in Leviticus:

‘Speak to the sons of Israel, and you shall say to them: When you come into the land which I am giving you, and you reap its harvest, you shall bring the sheaf, the firstfruits of your harvest, to the priest; and he shall lift up the sheaf before the Lord, to be accepted for you. On the day after the first the priest shall lift it up. And on the day on which you bring the sheaf you shall offer a sheep without blemish, a year old, as a whole burnt offering to the Lord; and its sacrifice, two tenths of fine flour mixed with oil, a sacrifice to the Lord, a fragrant odor to the Lord; and its drink offering, the fourth part of a hin of wine. And bread, and roasted new groats, you shall not eat until this very day, until you have brought the gifts to your God. It is a perpetual ordinance throughout your generations, in all your dwellings. And you shall count for yourselves, from the day after the sabbaths, from the day on which you bring the sheaf of the offering, seven full weeks; up to the day after the last week you shall count fifty days’ (Leviticus 23:10–16).

For the feast that truly saves is the death of Emmanuel on our behalf. He has paid our debts for us, and it is true that he himself takes away our sins and suffers pain for us, and by his bruise we were healed (Isaiah 53:4–5). For he nailed to his own cross the bond that stood against us, and in it he triumphed over those who once held sway on earth, I mean the rulers and authorities and the spiritual forces of wickedness, and, before all the rest, Satan (Colossians 2:14–15). And close beside it comes a feast no less than the first: the return to life from the dead, which shakes off corruption, shears away sin, and moves us into a new life, a life in holiness and incorruption, now that death has been abolished. For we have stripped off the old man and put on the new (Colossians 3:9–10), that is, Christ, or the way of life and the life that is in Christ. Look, then, look at the firstfruits of humanity being renewed, that is, Christ, as in the type of a sheaf, as the first yield of a field, as firstfruits from the crops, brought as a holy offering to God the Father. Or have we not sprung up in the world like ears of grain?

Palladius: Yes. That is why Christ himself spoke about us to the holy disciples (John 4:35–36): ‘Do you not say, “There are four months more, and the harvest comes”? Look, I tell you, lift up your eyes and see the fields, that they are white for…

title: Christ the firstfruits sheaf, raised on the third day
english: Palladius: …harvest already; and the reaper receives wages, and so does the gatherer.’ For he likens our condition to ears of grain and wheat.

Cyril: So, then, Christ is understood as a kind of firstfruits of the ears and as new fruit, in the form of a sheaf: the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:18), our road to the resurrection, the one who changes all things into newness and does away with oldness. ‘For the old things have passed away,’ it says, ‘behold, all things have become new; and if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation’ (2 Corinthians 5:17), as the Scriptures say. And the sheaf was lifted up before the Lord. For Emmanuel, raised from the dead, the new fruit of humanity and fruit as in incorruption, went up into heaven so that he might now appear for us before the face of God the Father (Hebrews 9:24). He did not, surely, bring himself into the Father's sight, for he is with him eternally and, as God, could never be parted from the Father. Rather, he brought into his sight, in himself, us who were outside his face and under wrath because of the transgression in Adam and the sin that had tyrannized over us. So in Christ we gain this as well: to come before the face of God. For he now counts us worthy of his regard, as sanctified. And see how the law also foreshadowed for us the time fitting for the resurrection, that is, the third day. For ‘on the day after the first,’ it says, ‘the priest shall lift up the sheaf before the Lord’ (Leviticus 23:11). The day reckoned from the first is surely the third: it says not ‘the morrow’ but ‘the day after the morrow.’ And Christ came back to life on the third day.
Palladius: True.

Cyril: And together with the sheaf a sheep without blemish is also offered up, with two tenths of fine flour brought with it, mixed again with oil. For the one who is portrayed, as it were, in the sheaf and the firstfruits of the crops is also taken as the firstfruits from a flock, a flock that lives, as it were, in the richness of grace and in the gladness of the Spirit. That is why it says that fine flour, oil and wine must be offered up with the sheep. Fine flour would be a sign of life, as we have said very often; oil, of richness; and wine, of gladness. And he is offered again as in bread, and in roasted groats. ‘Groats,’ it says, are pulse, because, I think, as they are ground they pour out around the mills of those who thresh them. Through this too Christ might be understood by us: the new dough, to whose form we have been shaped. And we have been commanded to keep the feasts after cleaning out the old leaven (1 Corinthians 5:7–8), so that we too may be named a new dough, in the likeness of the one who opened for us the whole road to newness of life, that is, Christ.
Palladius: Well said.
Cyril: He further commands that they must keep from the new crops and make nothing from them into food, but wait for the offering of the sheaf. For ‘of the new crop you shall not…
translator_notes: Cyril reads ‘the day after the first’ (Leviticus 23:11) as the third day, taking ἐπαύριον as ‘the day after the morrow’.

title: The two loaves of firstfruits and the new life after the resurrection
english: Cyril: …eat,’ it says, ‘until this very day, until you have brought the gifts to your God’ (Leviticus 23:14). For the fitting time to share in the new and undefiled life could only be, and very reasonably, the time when Emmanuel shone forth. Before him no one at all was able to refashion us into a new life; but he himself is, as it were, the firstfruits and the first of those created for incorruption, inasmuch as he appeared as a man and was in the flesh with us, because of his likeness to us. And at once the law introduced a clear foreshadowing of holy Pentecost for us, saying that seven weeks must be counted from the bringing of the sheaf. For after the day of the Savior's resurrection we who have believed count seven weeks together and keep the feast.
Palladius: How clear the account is!

Cyril: And that the time of our Savior's resurrection moves those sanctified in the Spirit and justified in faith into the power to bear the fruit of the new and genuine life, it showed clearly by saying straight away:

‘And you shall offer a new sacrifice to the Lord. From your dwelling you shall bring loaves as an offering, two loaves; the one loaf shall be of two tenths of fine flour; they shall be baked leavened, as firstfruits to the Lord. And with the loaves you shall bring seven lambs without blemish, a year old, and one calf from the herd, and two rams without blemish; and they shall be a whole burnt offering to the Lord, with their sacrifices and their drink offerings, a sacrifice, a fragrant odor to the Lord. And they shall offer one male goat from the goats for sin, and two lambs a year old for a sacrifice of salvation, with the loaves of the firstfruits. And the priest shall set them with the loaves of the firstfruits as an offering before the Lord, with the two lambs; they shall be holy to the Lord; they shall belong to the priest who offers them. And you shall proclaim this day a day of assembly; it shall be holy to you; you shall do no work of service on it. It is a perpetual ordinance throughout your generations, in all your dwelling’ (Leviticus 23:16–21).

For Emmanuel is the firstfruits and, as it were, the first yield of the creation being refashioned into newness; and he is understood to be first among us, as bread and new dough. And we, taking as it were the path to the same thing, have been called a new dough too, in likeness to him. The bread brought from the new crops would be a clear type of this as well. But it says that not one loaf but two must be offered; for the peoples are two, even if they appear brought together into unity through Christ the mediator. Yet ‘they shall be baked leavened,’ it says. And what is the riddle? Come, let us say, after looking well, as far as we can, into the depth of the law. Is it consistent to understand leaven here as the leaven of wickedness and falsehood? Then how is that not foolishness? For how could we still count as rid of evil those who have been refashioned for the newness of the gospel way of life? Or how could…

title: The good leaven of the Gospel and growth toward maturity in Christ
english: Cyril: …this be understood as newness? And how could some still be called a new dough, if a remnant of leaven stays in them and they have not wholly parted from unholy and loathsome wickedness? We must therefore conceive, by the reasoning that fits such contemplations, of another kind of leaven, one that has nothing in itself to be blamed, but is rather even admired in the inspired Scripture. So the Savior likens the renowned and beneficial power of the divine and gospel training to leaven, saying: ‘The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until the whole was leavened’ (Matthew 13:33). For the life-giving working of the gospel training, sinking into mind and heart, changes soul and body and spirit, as it were, into its own quality. So it would be fitting to suppose that the peoples are leavened with such leaven, brought as they are in the form of the loaves, each of two tenths; the type depicting for us in a riddle the twofold, as it were, character of the training.
Palladius: What exactly do you mean?
Cyril: Would you not say, Palladius, that through a twofold training, of the law and of the gospel, we shall be holy and acceptable to God, and so go forward into a new and choice life?
Palladius: I would.

Cyril: The Savior himself made this clear to us, saying: ‘Therefore I said to you that every scribe who has been made a disciple in the kingdom of heaven is like a rich man who brings out of his treasure things new and old’ (Matthew 13:52). For those whose mind knows what was decreed through Moses and has been filled with that ancient commandment given in types, and who on top of it have grown rich in the new knowledge of the gospel, can boast from then on, I think, of a twofold training.
Palladius: You have spoken rightly.

Cyril: But the multitude of those prepared for newness of life was not depicted for us in the loaves alone. The law further commands that seven lambs be brought, with the one calf and two rams; and plainly a drink offering follows the victims, that is, wine poured out, a fourth part of a hin, which is six xestai, as it is called in our language. So the seven lambs in turn would be a type of the flock of believers, a flock still in infancy in Christ, for the lamb is a symbol of infancy, yet advancing, as in spiritual strength and manliness, to perfection and to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ (Ephesians 4:13).
Palladius: How do you mean?

Cyril: Having named the lambs, he then puts the calf in between and adds the rams. The lambs would be a type of the flock; the calf, of strength and manliness, for the animal is sturdy; and the rams, finally, of full-grown age. So believers, through their habit of manfully mastering what is…
translator_notes: Matthew 13:52: Cyril's text reads ‘a rich man’ where the Gospel reads ‘a householder’.

title: Perfection in deed and knowledge, and burial with Christ in baptism
english: Cyril: …more earthly, leap up to the perfection understood as in Christ. For the rams, full-grown in age, mark very well in themselves the measure of spiritual perfection. And the rams are two, for perfection in Christ is in a way twofold in us, understood as in deed and in knowledge. ‘For whoever does and teaches,’ it says, ‘he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven’ (Matthew 5:19). And wine is poured over the victims again; for gladness must surely follow those who are eager to speed toward the perfection understood as in Christ. ‘For wine,’ it says, ‘gladdens the heart of man’ (Psalm 104:15).

And a male goat was slaughtered for sin, and two lambs are brought besides with the loaves as a sacrifice of salvation. What is the meaning of this in turn? Emmanuel died for our sins, depicted in the goat; and he makes holy and acceptable our new life of newness, our change into new dough, and the offering and consecration, reaching to soul and body, which we are accustomed to undergo, all but dying together with the one who for our sake was among the dead, so that we may live with him. Paul the wise writes something of this kind to us, saying: ‘Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried with him, then, through baptism into his death, so that just as Christ was raised through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life’ (Romans 6:3–4). So he himself was slain for our sins, and we too were buried with him, undergoing a death that is not bodily, but putting to death the members that are on the earth (Colossians 3:5), no longer living to the world, but rather to Christ, and through him to the Father.

See, then, the lambs dying together with the goat as it is slain, and the loaves burned together with them; for our consecration is acceptable, and the new life of the gospel is a fragrant odor, molded in some way together with the sufferings of Christ and running on in imitation of him. ‘For if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him; if we die with him, we shall also live with him’ (2 Timothy 2:11–12); ‘and if we are sharers in the sufferings, we too shall have a part in the glory.’ Such an offering, it says, is rightly called a sacrifice of salvation. For Christ saves those for whom he endured the slaughter, since he takes them out of sin and makes those buried with him and dying with him superior to death and corruption, in the way already described.
Palladius: How deep the account is, and how obscure the matter of the law!
Cyril: It is a riddle, Palladius, and, as it were, a dim shadow-sketch of fine and finely carved ideas.
Palladius: Well said.
Cyril: The law, then, named three seasons in which it would be fitting for us to keep feasts. For ‘three,’ it says, ‘…
translator_notes: The quotation ‘For if we suffer with him…’ blends 2 Timothy 2:11–12 with a clause close to Romans 8:17 (‘if we are sharers in the sufferings…’).

title: The third feast in the seventh month, a figure of the end
english: Cyril: …times in the year you shall keep a feast for me’ (Exodus 23:14). Now that our account of two of them has been sufficient, do you want us to say what the third is, and for what it is kept? You surely learned the reason for each. The one was fittingly kept because Christ, who endured death for the salvation of us all, has saved us; the other because he destroyed corruption, came back to life, and renewed us into a new life. And the time of the first is, among the months of the year, the first and at the beginning; the time of the second is its near neighbor, joined right to it, the time when it was natural for the reaping iron to hurry to the ears of grain and for the other kinds of seed to be gathered in, for the crops of the fields are countless. Come, then, let us say what is fitting about the season of the third feast too, inquiring closely how and on what grounds it must be accomplished. Let us ask the law for the knowledge of this, and take it from the sacred Scriptures themselves; for so our account would move toward the truth. Do I not seem to you to say and to have thought this through rightly?
Palladius: Entirely so.

Cyril: It is written, then, in Leviticus: ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel, saying: In the seventh month, on the first of the month, you shall have a rest, an everlasting memorial of trumpets, a holy assembly to the Lord. You shall do no work of service, and you shall offer whole burnt offerings to the Lord’ (Leviticus 23:23–25).

The seventh month seems to us to hint at the time of the consummation and of the last things. For in the seventh month, my friend, the produce of the fields is not to be gathered from here and there to the threshing floor; it is fitting that it be already shut up in each man's storehouses. The season of good harvests has passed, the beginning of winter is already rising, plants wither and flowers fade. Come, then, let us transfer what belongs to the season to ourselves and say this: as this age is already creeping toward its end, and the time hangs over us, as it were, and is about to break in, the time when the lovers of sin must be punished, each one, if he is wise, will heap up the fruit of his own labors and bring it into the treasuries above. He will remember Christ saying: ‘Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal; but rather store up treasures in heaven’ (Matthew 6:19–20). So, since, now that Christ has been raised, the words of the holy teachers of the mysteries bring us to remember the consummation (for they have cried aloud up and down, ‘It is the last hour’ (1 John 2:18)), let what belongs to each, it says, be gathered from now on into the treasuries above. But ‘on the new moon,’ it says, ‘of the month in which you shut up the crops, you shall have a rest, a memorial of trumpets.’ For each one stores up the good things won by his own sweat, and will take thought and care for the delight and rest that last forever, remembering that, as the inspired Paul says…
translator_notes: Leviticus 23:24: the print reads ‘for us’ (ἡμῖν) inside the Lord's words; the Septuagint reads ‘for you’ (ὑμῖν), which is followed here.

title: The trumpet of the Lord's coming and the Day of Atonement
english: Cyril: …‘The Lord himself will come down from heaven with a word of command, with the voice of an archangel and with the trumpet of God’ (1 Thessalonians 4:16). ‘For the trumpet will sound,’ it says, ‘and the dead will be raised incorruptible’ (1 Corinthians 15:52). ‘For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what was done through the body, in keeping with what he has done, whether good or bad’ (2 Corinthians 5:10). Let us remember, then, this holy and most fearful trumpet, when the most glorious feast of the saints also comes, a holy assembly, as those who lived in hope at last receive as their lot a rich repayment for their splendid deeds of valor. We must therefore, rising through our thoughts on these things to great goodness, cease from every work that is known to profit nothing at all, or rather to stain. For this, I think, is what Paul too said wisely to us: ‘The time has been shortened from now on, so that those who have wives may be as though they had none, and those who use this world as though not misusing it’ (1 Corinthians 7:29, 31).
Palladius: So it seems.

Cyril: Then it says: ‘On the tenth of this seventh month is the Day of Atonement; it shall be a holy assembly for you. And you shall humble your souls and offer whole burnt offerings to the Lord. You shall do no work on this very day, for it is a Day of Atonement for you, to make atonement for you before the Lord your God. Every soul that is not humbled on this very day shall be destroyed from its people. And every soul that does any work on this very day, that soul shall perish from its people. You shall do no work of service; it is a perpetual ordinance throughout your generations, in all your dwellings. It shall be a sabbath of sabbaths for you, and you shall humble your souls; from the ninth of the month, from evening to evening, you shall keep your sabbaths’ (Leviticus 23:27–32).

He said that there must be humbling and fasting, the offering of whole burnt offerings, and also a ceasing from every work. By the fasting he sketched the putting to death of the desires of the flesh; by the whole burnt offerings, our dedication as a fragrant odor, not in part but entirely and completely; and by the rest, and the command to withdraw wholly from works, he signified, aptly, that it is fitting to accomplish nothing earthly any longer. Or will you not think that those who have already come through to the close of the ages, who remember the holy trumpet at the last, who keep the judge in mind, and who for this reason are carrying the wealth of their spiritual harvest into the treasuries above from now on, must put pleasures to death and be seen to be above the passions of the body, must now make the ways of goodness fragrant to God, and must go far off and make it their habit to separate themselves from pursuits that end in vanity? These would be, I think, the things in this world, and the wicked distraction of life.
Palladius: I shall think so; how could I not?

title: From putting earthly members to death to the joy of Tabernacles
english: Cyril: Well then, will not those who are above the passions, and who put to death the members that are on the earth, fornication, impurity, passion, evil desire (Colossians 3:5), be dedicated to God as a fragrant odor and stand in the rank of the whole burnt offerings, making the matter a kind of ransom and propitiation for their own souls?
Palladius: Very much so.

Cyril: So the lawgiver called the day of fasting the Day of Atonement, and very rightly and lawfully, since it puts to death the flesh and what belongs to it and makes the ways of virtue fragrant. And whoever does not cease from all worldly work will be, utterly and in every way, in the worst of evils. This he showed clearly by saying that whoever neither fasts nor offers the whole burnt offering, and whoever outrages the law about the days of rest, will be destroyed from his people. And by saying that the time for these things is a sabbath of sabbaths, he left us to understand that there is from now on a rest of rests, that is, a laying aside of works wholly and in full measure, plainly of works that lead to wickedness and sin. And now that this age is coming to its close and the time is all but growing old, what share at all could the pursuit of vanity still have in us? Shall we not rather set our minds on better things, keeping the rest most pleasing to God and withdrawing entirely from our own distractions?
Palladius: Well said.

Cyril: And again he lays down the law: ‘And on the fifteenth day,’ it says, ‘of this seventh month, when you have finished gathering the produce of the land, keep a feast to the Lord seven days. On the first day there shall be a rest, and on the eighth day a rest. And on the first day you shall take the beautiful fruit of a tree, and branches of palms, and thick boughs of trees, and willows, and branches of chaste-tree from the brook; and you shall rejoice before the Lord your God seven days in the year. It is a perpetual ordinance throughout your generations. In the seventh month you shall keep it’ (Leviticus 23:39–41).

Do you perceive, then, that when the produce of the fields has been gathered into the storehouse and each man's crops have been well collected, the far-famed Feast of Tabernacles is very near, hinting at the life in paradise and restoring man to a share in what was at the beginning? For we say that the Feast of Tabernacles is the spiritual and truer joining-together of human bodies, and their return to life out of the corruption that came between, into incorruption. And the first day is a rest, and so is the eighth. For before the transgression at the beginning, when the most wicked sin had not yet fallen upon us and laid on us its yoke, truly heavy and hard to bear, we led a life in paradise that was free and unbound and without any toil, as in Adam, the beginning and root of the race. But when Christ came to dwell among us, the time of toil that came between ran back to what was at the beginning on the eighth day, that is, after the law’s…

title: Rest at Tabernacles and Christ the stream for the thirsty
english: Cyril: …sabbath rest, that is, the fulfillment of the time of the law; and, having driven the heavy and profane yoke of sin away from our own souls, we have ceased from all wickedness, as Christ calls us to this through faith and says, ‘Come to me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest’ (Matthew 11:28). So the first day of the week is rest, and it points to man’s time at the beginning. And the eighth day is likewise rest, the day on which Christ came back to life, having nailed to his own cross the bond that stood against us (Colossians 2:14). One died for all (2 Corinthians 5:14), so that he might take us out of death and sins and free us from punishment and toil, and so that through him we might gain the rest that was at the beginning.

‘On the first day,’ it says, ‘they shall take fine fruit of a tree, and branches of palm trees, and the other boughs’ (Leviticus 23:40). Through this one may understand, as though the thing itself were crying it aloud, that in Christ God again grants us the delights of paradise, though in the meantime we had slipped away from them through the transgression at the beginning. We were thrust out in Adam, but we have been brought back in through Christ. You have heard him, I suppose, saying to the robber who hung beside him, ‘Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise’ (Luke 23:43). For Christ has turned back the turning sword (Genesis 3:24), and the way in now stands open to those who have believed, as he reshapes all things into what they were at the beginning and restores them to what they once were.

The branches come from evergreen plants, and they signify in themselves the unbroken continuance of grace and the unfading, so to speak, quality of our hope. For ‘the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable,’ as it is written (Romans 11:29). And the delight of the saints truly has no end. The wise Isaiah too will cry out, saying, ‘Everlasting gladness shall be over their heads; praise and everlasting gladness shall overtake them; pain, grief and sighing have fled away’ (Isaiah 35:10).

Along with the decrees about the feast, it is somehow added that they must rejoice from the torrent. For he said that on the last day of the week, that is, on the eighth, they were to draw water from the torrent, and that in this way the believers would rejoice. And Christ is a spiritual and heavenly torrent, watering the souls of those who worship him with streams from above. That is why he also said through the voice of the prophets, ‘Behold, I turn toward them like a river of peace, and like a torrent flooding them with the glory of the nations’ (Isaiah 66:12). Somewhere, too, the inspired David cried out for us to the God and Father of all: ‘How you have multiplied your mercy, O God! The sons of men shall hope in the shelter of your wings. They shall be drunk with the richness of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight’ (Psalm 36:7–8). For it would be very fitting indeed for the citizens of paradise to share richly in Christ and to rejoice in the abundant gifts of the Spirit.
Palladius: Fitting indeed, and you are right.
Cyril: Notice how the feast was kept in Jerusalem alone, and how it was altogether necessary…
translator_notes: Leviticus 23:40: Cyril gives the third kind of branch as ‘the other boughs’; the Greek Bible names thick boughs and willows.
On the drawing of water from the torrent on the eighth day: Cyril reads the closing words of Leviticus 23:40 in the Greek (‘from the brook, to rejoice’) as a command to draw water.

title: The heavenly Jerusalem and the continual sacrifice
english: Cyril: …for those from all Judea to gather in it. This too would be a sign that all who have lived a glorious and well-approved life must be gathered into the city above, the heavenly Jerusalem (Hebrews 12:22), to be with Christ there and to keep the feast with him. But for those who are still unbelieving, who do not accept the grace of the resurrection but have rather set aside so august and deep a mystery, destruction is the penalty laid up: to be in every evil then, wholly and altogether. For they will go down into punishment. And the prophet Zechariah would be a faithful witness to this, when he says, ‘And it shall be that whoever of all the tribes of the earth do not go up to Jerusalem to worship the King, the Lord Almighty, they too shall be added to those. And if the tribe of Egypt does not go up nor come there, upon them too shall be the fall with which the Lord will strike all the nations, whoever does not go up to keep the feast of Tabernacles’ (Zechariah 14:17–18). So we shall reckon the thrice-longed-for feast of Tabernacles to be, I suppose, the resurrection of all bodies, which have Christ as their firstfruits. For he has been called the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:18), and he truly is.
Palladius: Your thought is most correct.
Cyril: But know this, at least.
Palladius: What is that? What do you mean?

Cyril: In the oracles of the law that we have just brought forward, there are named the continual sacrifice, and the new moon too, and the sacred rites on the sabbaths, and also the fast, and besides these the much-desired feast of Tabernacles.
