And everywhere, with each of the things named, the law added, ‘You shall offer whole burnt offerings to the Lord.’ But what the manner of our sacrifices should be, those fitting for the new moon, and for the sabbaths too, and for the fast, and those to be offered at the feast of Tabernacles itself, or what exactly the continual sacrifice is, the lawgiver passed over in silence in Leviticus. In Numbers, however, he broadens the account of these things, as it were, and has set it out in very fine detail. Shall we take each of them in turn, as far as we can, and speak of it?
Palladius: By all means.

Cyril: It is written as follows (Numbers 28:1–7): ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Command the sons of Israel, and say to them: My gifts, my presents, my offerings for a fragrant aroma you shall take care to offer to me at my feasts. And you shall say to them: These are the offerings that you shall bring to the Lord: two unblemished lambs a year old each day, as a continual whole burnt offering. The one lamb you shall offer in the morning, and the second lamb you shall offer toward evening; and you shall offer a tenth of an ephah of fine flour for a sacrifice, mixed with a quarter of a hin of oil. It is a continual whole burnt offering, the sacrifice that was made on Mount Sinai for a fragrant aroma to the Lord. And its drink offering, a quarter of a hin for each lamb; in the holy place you shall pour…
translator_notes: Numbers 28:7: the print notes a variant, ‘in the vessel’, for ‘in the holy place’.

title: The daily lambs and the Church's unceasing offering
english: Cyril: …a drink offering of strong drink to the Lord. And the second lamb you shall offer toward evening; according to its sacrifice and according to its drink offering you shall offer it, for a fragrant aroma to the Lord’ (Numbers 28:7–8). Do you understand, then, how the divine law insists to us here that the offering up of sacrifices is most fitting at the feasts? For I think we must at them, wholly and in every way, make the ways of the life in Christ give off a fragrance to God, presenting them as if in the rank of incense, and bringing ourselves to God as a fragrant whole burnt offering, according, I think, to the saying that is so rightly spoken: ‘Present your bodies, then, as a living sacrifice, holy, well pleasing to God, which is your reasonable service’ (Romans 12:1).

He says, very well, that the continual sacrifice must be completed with one lamb slaughtered in the morning and another toward evening, with fine flour burned together with them, and oil and wine brought in addition. For at every time, without ceasing, from beginning to end, in the holy tent, that is, in the Church, we give off a fragrance in Christ through every virtue. The burning of the lambs in the morning and toward evening would be, again, an outline of him who for us and on our behalf rises up to the Father as a fragrant aroma, and carries up with him, as it were, the life of those who have believed in him, a life that is cheerful, as resting in the hope of sure glory and kingdom. And besides this it shows that we must rejoice in the delights that last forever; and a sign of such a life would be fine flour moistened with oil and soaked in wine.

So the thing is a sacrifice of salvation, like the one Moses performed on Mount Sinai. It is written in Exodus, when he had laid down the laws of God, who rules all things, on everything that was to be done: ‘Rising early in the morning,’ it says, ‘Moses built an altar on the mountain, and twelve stones for the twelve tribes of Israel; and he sent the young men of the sons of Israel, and they offered whole burnt offerings and a sacrifice of salvation to God, calves’ (Exodus 24:4–5). The meaning of the sacrifice will make no difference, I think, whether the victims are lambs or whether perhaps they are called calves. For in both the type of innocence is kept, and one would apply it above all to the person of Christ, who says through the voice of Jeremiah, ‘But I was like an innocent lamb led to be slaughtered, and I did not know’ (Jeremiah 11:19). And if someone should choose to say, in another way, that the morning and evening sacrifice in the holy tent was conceived with a view to the time of mankind, that it was fragrant before the transgression in Adam, and that it became so again in the last times and in Christ, and in the life understood in him, he would not be wide of the mark, and his reasoning would be wise; for that is how the matter stands by its nature.
Palladius: I am persuaded.

Cyril: He at once defines the sacrifices on the sabbath, saying (Numbers 28:9): ‘And on the day of the sabbaths you shall bring two unblemished lambs a year old, and two tenths of fine flour mixed with oil for a sacrifice, and…
translator_notes: Exodus 24:4: Cyril’s text has the altar ‘on the mountain’; the Greek Bible reads ‘under the mountain’.

title: Sabbath offerings, the true Sabbath, and the new moon
english: Cyril: …a drink offering. These are the whole burnt offerings of the sabbaths, on the sabbaths, besides the continual whole burnt offering and its drink offering’ (Numbers 28:9–10). The manner of the sacrifice is no different from the one we have just described; these follow it step by step, so as to differ in nothing. But notice this, my friend: the continual sacrifice is a perpetual service and is performed every day according to the law, but that of the sabbaths is not offered every day, only on the sabbaths themselves. So, lest they think the continual sacrifice offered every day enough, and grow somehow careless about bringing the offerings of the sabbaths, he necessarily added, ‘This is the whole burnt offering of the sabbaths on the sabbaths, besides the continual whole burnt offering and its drink offering’ (Numbers 28:10).
Palladius: So it is settled, then, that besides the continual sacrifice the sacrifice of the sabbaths too is offered according to the law?

Cyril: It is settled; it is not right to doubt it. For we too, keeping sabbath in Christ and having entered into his rest (Hebrews 4:10), shall offer to God the things of spiritual fragrance in double measure, as it were, if indeed it is true that the boast of righteousness under the law was fragrant to those of old. For the law is spiritual (Romans 7:14), and ‘the commandment is holy and just and good’ (Romans 7:12), in the words of the blessed Paul; yet the life in Christ stands higher, and the sabbath-keeping in the spirit is better in fragrance than the righteousness under the law.
Palladius: Well said.

Cyril: He adds to these: ‘And at the new moons you shall bring a whole burnt offering to the Lord: two calves from the herd, and one ram, seven unblemished lambs a year old; three tenths of fine flour mixed with oil for the one calf, and two tenths of fine flour mixed with oil for the one ram; a tenth of fine flour mixed with oil for each lamb, a sacrifice, a fragrant aroma, an offering to the Lord. Their drink offering shall be half a hin for the one calf, and a third of a hin for the one ram, and a quarter of a hin of wine for the one lamb. This is the whole burnt offering month by month, through the months of the year; and one male goat from the goats for sin to the Lord; it shall be offered besides the continual whole burnt offering, and its drink offering’ (Numbers 28:11–15).

A perpetual and unceasing sacrifice, then, as it were: each month, besides the daily one, which is the continual sacrifice, there is also the one at the new moons. The account of them, again, will not be of one kind only, for the riddle is quite clear. The spiritual and truer new moon may fittingly be understood as the new age in Christ, since the first one, under the law, has passed away. But in another way the new moon would also be for us a type of the age that is to come after this one and is all but here, though it has its beginning in the resurrection of Christ. Through it we have passed over into newness, enriched with the Spirit as the pledge of grace (2 Corinthians 1:22), and holding a sure hope of the life that leads to…

title: The new moon: dying and living with Christ
english: Cyril: …incorruptible life, as we are transformed in blessedness and holiness back to what was at the beginning, and, going backward as it were, are conformed to the age to come. What, then, is the sacrifice that befits the new moons, that is, the spiritual new moon in Christ, and the life of the age to come? To die to God, and no longer to live held fast by sins, but to depart altogether from the more earthly way of life, so that we may live with Christ. So too the inspired Paul writes to those sanctified in the Spirit, justified in Christ, and taught the powers of the age to come, saying, ‘If you died in Christ, why, as though you were living in the world, do you submit to decrees?’ (Colossians 2:20). And again: ‘For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, our life, appears, then you too will appear with him in glory’ (Colossians 3:3–4).

See, then, how those who are used to being well approved die sacredly to God in differing measures of spiritual vigor, and at once win the rewards of goodness. For two calves are sacrificed, and one ram with them, and seven lambs without blemish. Through all these the multitude of the saints is described for us: as excelling in the highest virtue, through the calves; as sitting a little lower, in the second rank as it were, as in the ram; and again as in the lesser and humbler virtue, in the lambs. The calves are two, for the peoples are two; and one ram between them, because of the union of the two into one in Christ. The lambs, again, are seven, for the people of the saints is in the most perfect fullness. And since they are two, and yet one by spiritual union, the multitude may fittingly be understood as most perfect. For the flock of those who believe is very broad, both in the simplicity that is in Christ and in the childlikeness that is after his pattern.

Notice how three tenths of fine flour are set apart for the one calf, and oil and wine in half a hin, that is, six pints. For the ram, two tenths of fine flour, and what is poured on in a third of a hin. For each of the lambs, one tenth of fine flour is the sacrifice, and a quarter of a hin is the drink offering, that is, oil and wine. For in equal weight with each one’s labors, and with his powers in virtue, the measure of life will be allotted by the one who judges justly: of life in renown and blessedness, I mean, and of union with God, and of spiritual gladness. Have we not said very often that the fine flour serves as a type of life, the oil of richness, and the wine of spiritual gladness?
Palladius: Yes, indeed.

Cyril: A male goat, again, is added to the sacrifices, slaughtered for sins, as a type of Christ. For our sacrifice is acceptable and pleasing to God because of the saving passion of Christ. And this, I think, is what the Savior himself said to the holy apostles: ‘Without me you can do nothing’ (John 15:5). So Christ’s fragrance is of necessity added to our fragrances, blending itself in a way with ours and carrying them up with it to the Father…
translator_notes: ‘Six pints’: Cyril reckons half a hin as six xestai (Roman sextarii), each a little under an English pint.

title: Trumpets, Atonement, and the dwindling count of calves at Tabernacles
english: Cyril: …For we are acceptable in no other way than through Christ alone.
Palladius: Excellently said.

Cyril: These, then, are the offerings for us on the sabbaths and the new moons. ‘And in the seventh month,’ it says, ‘on the first day of the month, there shall be a holy convocation for you. You shall do no work of service. It shall be for you a day of signaling. And you shall offer whole burnt offerings for a fragrant aroma to the Lord: one calf from the herd, and one ram, seven unblemished lambs a year old’ (Numbers 29:1–2). There are three tenths of fine flour for the calf, two again for the ram, and one for each of the lambs, with what is poured on, oil, I mean, and wine, following in proportion: in a half, a third and a quarter of the Hebrew hin. What the force of the feast should be taken to be, he hinted by saying, ‘It shall be for you a day of signaling.’ For it signals to us the last trumpet, sounded by the angel’s voice, at which all the dead will rise (1 Corinthians 15:52), and those in the tombs will be raised (John 5:28), as we have said before. He also commanded that on the tenth of the same month, the day of the fast, which describes in itself the putting to death of the desires of the flesh and the departure from earthly passions, the same sacrifice must be performed in the same way as on the first (Numbers 29:7–8). How the force of these rites stands, by the account that fits their contemplation, we have said sufficiently.
Palladius: I will remember.

Cyril: He lays down, again, what sacrifices we are to offer as fitting for the feast of Tabernacles, and says: ‘And on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, so called, it shall be holy for you. You shall do no work of service. And you shall keep it as a feast to the Lord seven days, and you shall bring whole burnt offerings, an offering to the Lord for a fragrant aroma: on the first day thirteen calves from the herd, two rams, fourteen lambs a year old; they shall be without blemish. Their sacrifices shall be fine flour mixed with oil: three tenths for each calf, for the thirteen calves, and two tenths for each ram, for the two rams; a tenth for each lamb, for the fourteen lambs; and one male goat from the goats for sin, besides the continual whole burnt offering; their sacrifices and their drink offerings’ (Numbers 29:12–16). Then, with one calf taken away each day, the sacrifice goes on in the same manner and measure. For the rams are two, the lambs fourteen, and the goat one. And so on the second day twelve calves were brought; eleven on the third, and ten on the fourth; nine on the fifth, eight on the sixth, and seven on the seventh (Numbers 29:17–32). Do you understand, then, that each day the number of the calves alone decreases, while the number of the rams stays equal, and so too that of the lambs, and the fine flour and what is poured out?
Palladius: And what does this mean, my friend? Why were there thirteen calves at the beginning, decreasing…
translator_notes: Numbers 29:12: Cyril’s text reads ‘of the seventh month, so called, it shall be holy’ where the Greek Bible has ‘there shall be a holy convocation’.

title: The dwindling calves as Israel's training under the law
english: Palladius: …by one taken away each day, while the rams, again, are two and the lambs fourteen, with a goat added to the victims?

Cyril: The sense of what was decreed is hard to make out, Palladius, and the matter is obscure by nature. But I will try, as far as I can, to say what has come to my mind. You yourself will adjust it for the better if I do not shoot straight at the mark.
Palladius: I will.

Cyril: Well, then, the divine oracle seems to portray for us both the training under the law of those from Israel and the calling of those brought in through faith to sanctification. The riddle of the sacrifice shows, I think, that there were two periods in which the flocks of the Jews may be understood to have been trained toward the knowledge of God and into the way of life under the law. And what would these periods be, if not surely the one in which Moses was still alive, and Joshua and the judges, and the one in which the prophets came, down to John the Baptist, who had something more, as the Savior said (Matthew 11:9), than an apostle’s mission and a prophet’s ministry? But the sacred Scripture hints that in the two periods there were some who walked the path of life praised in the law, yet not in equal measure, nor at all closely alike in strength and spiritual vigor. Some, perhaps, were of the highest measure, of which the calf would be a type; others again of the measure understood as middle, and of this too the ram would be a sign; and a third group besides, of the measure that falls a little short and sits lower, as one can see, of course, in the lambs, as to bodily size. For is not a ram smaller than a calf, and does not the lamb fall below the ram in size?
Palladius: Yes, of course.

Cyril: So the animals named would be a very clear type of the measure of each person, clearly of his measure in goodness. And since what always stands out and is choice is somehow fewer in number than the second and the third, for it is rare, that is why there are thirteen calves, [two] rams, and fourteen lambs. And since we say that the rams are two, the number of the victims is doubled: instead of seven lambs, there are fourteen [lambs], and the rams are two. Or is it not likely that many became august and holy, and could boast of being blameless according to the righteousness in the law? Just as, of course, the divine evangelist has written for us about Zechariah and Elizabeth: ‘They were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless’ (Luke 1:6).

Palladius: Yes; and God somewhere reproached the mother of the Jews, saying, ‘How has the faithful city Zion become a harlot, she who was full of judgment, in whom righteousness lodged?’ (Isaiah 1:21).
Cyril: There was, then, a righteousness according to the law, by which it is likely that some became most approved in obedience to God…
translator_notes: The print reads ‘ten rams’ where Numbers 29 and Cyril’s own next sentence have two; ‘[two]’ follows the sense.
The print reads ‘fourteen calves’ in ‘instead of seven lambs, fourteen calves’; the sense requires ‘lambs’, given in brackets.

title: The law leads to Christ, our true Sabbath rest
english: Cyril: …though the law did not at all bring them to perfection in sanctification.
Palladius: Well said.

Cyril: So calves and rams and lambs were sacrificed to God, signifying the calling of Israel, as in the highest, the middle, and those still lesser. And the number of the calves kept growing smaller, since the chosen, the outstanding and the most approved kept failing, as the times kept suffering from their scarcity, up to the seventh day, that is, the coming of our Savior, in which at last the sabbath-keeping in the spirit, and rest from works that lead to sin, sprang up. For we have been justified in Christ, as the present age already flows down toward its end. And this would again be a sign of it, that for us the sabbath lies at the end of the whole week. That is why, it says, the law wisely stops the bringing of the ancient victims at the sabbath, that is, the calling under the law and the service according to it, and brings in, as it were, in its place the calling in Christ, saying: ‘And on the eighth day there shall be a closing festival for you. You shall do no work of service on it, and you shall bring a whole burnt offering, an offering for a fragrant aroma to the Lord: one calf, one ram, seven unblemished lambs a year old. Their sacrifices and their drink offerings for the calf and the ram and the lambs, according to their number, according to their rule; and one male goat from the goats for sin, besides the continual whole burnt offering. Their sacrifices and their drink offerings: these you shall offer to the Lord at your feasts, besides your vows, and your freewill offerings, and your whole burnt offerings, and your sacrifices, and your drink offerings, and your offerings of salvation’ (Numbers 29:35–39).

Do you hear the law saying plainly, ‘It is a closing festival’? For the worship in shadows and the training in type came to their close on the eighth day, on which Christ came back to life, and the time of circumcision in the spirit (Romans 2:29) broke in. The ancient multitude of those who had been called was shut out, sick with the charge of unbelief, and in its place there sprang up, as it were, the new people: excelling in spiritual strength, and that is the calf; perfectly approved, as in the fullness of maturity, and that is the ram; and having the choice beauty of the childlikeness and innocence that is in Christ, and that is the lamb, even if it is understood as in the most perfect multitude; for saying that the lambs are seven surely hints at this. And the goat follows too. For it is in Christ that the people is approved through faith, as it goes up to God as a fragrant aroma, as we have often said.
Palladius: So it is.

Cyril: That we shall keep sabbath in Christ, coming to rest, in that we must cease from worldly pursuits and no longer bear earthly care, but rather delight in the Lord, as it is written (Psalm 37:4), and have with him the choice inheritance, he will make clear when he says in…

title: The jubilee release and the inheritance at the last trumpet
english: Cyril: …Leviticus to Moses, the revealer of sacred things: ‘Speak to the sons of Israel, and say to them: When you come into the land that I am giving you, and you give the land that I am giving you rest, sabbaths to the Lord: six years you shall sow your field, and six years you shall prune your vineyard and gather in its fruit; but in the seventh year, sabbaths. It shall be a rest for your land, sabbaths to the Lord. You shall not sow your field, and you shall not prune your vineyard, and what springs up of itself in your field you shall not reap, and the grapes of your consecration you shall not gather; it shall be a year of rest for the land. And the sabbaths of the land shall be food for you, and for your servant, and for your maidservant, and for your hired worker, and for the sojourner who stays with you; and for your cattle and for the wild animals in your land all its produce shall be for food. And you shall count for yourself seven rests of years, seven years seven times; and you shall have seven weeks of years, forty-nine years. And you shall proclaim with the sound of the trumpet in all your land, in the seventh month, on the tenth of the month; on the day of atonement you shall proclaim with the trumpet in all your land. And you shall sanctify the year, the fiftieth year, and proclaim release in the land to all who live in it. It shall be a year of release; it shall be a signal for you, and each one shall go back to his possession, and each shall go back to his family’ (Leviticus 25:2–10).

Do you understand, then, how the law allows plowing and sowing and tending vineyards before the seventh year? But it commanded release from care for these things in the seventh. For we are released as we keep sabbath in Christ, having removed our care from earthly things and departed altogether from vain distractions. ‘Seven weeks of years,’ that is, ages of ages, we shall spend among goods that are ready and set before us, delighting, plainly, in the spiritual things that come from God, and keeping festival. For there will be a time of release for all of us throughout the whole inhabited world, the time at the end, when each will also run to his own possession, that is, to the portion that befits him and has been allotted by God. For as there is a difference in the life of the saints, so also in their rewards, since God measures out the repayment in proportion to each one’s good deeds. He also makes mention of the trumpet that proclaims such things. For our time of sabbath-keeping, in Christ, plainly, and of release and of the giving of the inheritance, is the return to life from the dead, which will come in its own time through the trumpet and the voice of an angel (1 Thessalonians 4:16), in which the shining multitude of the saints will hear Christ saying, ‘Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world’ (Matthew 25:34). May we too attain it, by the grace and loving-kindness of our Lord and God and Savior Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
